question: Which class of lipids is the primary long-term energy storage form in adipose tissue?
cited_learning_objective: List the major classes of lipids, and their basic function

options.rationale: Triacylglycerols (triglycerides) are described as the primary storage form of fats in adipose tissue and used for energy, heat, and insulation.
Phospholipids are membrane components and signaling molecules; they are not the main storage form and would be correct only if the question asked about membrane structure.
Sphingolipids are membrane components, especially in nervous tissue; they are not the primary energy storage form and would be correct only if the stem asked about neural membranes.
Eicosanoids are signaling molecules derived from arachidonic acid; they are not storage lipids and would be correct only if the question asked about cell signaling.
Isoprenoids/steroids function as hormones and membrane components; they are not the main adipose storage form and would be correct only if the stem targeted steroid hormones.

question: A fatty acid abbreviated 18:1(9) has which structural features?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the basic structure of fatty acids and be able to give the abbreviation of fatty acids based on chain length and saturation

options.text: 18 carbons and one double bond at carbon 9
options.rationale: The notation 18:1(9) denotes 18 carbons with one double bond located at carbon 9 from the carboxyl end.

options.text: 18 carbons and one double bond at carbon 1
options.rationale: A double bond at carbon 1 would be written as (1); this option is incorrect unless the position were specified as 1.

options.text: 18 carbons and two double bonds at carbons 9 and 12
options.rationale: Two double bonds would be indicated as 18:2; this option would be correct only if the abbreviation were 18:2(9,12).

options.text: 16 carbons and one double bond at carbon 9
options.rationale: This describes a 16:1(9) fatty acid, not 18:1(9); it would be correct only if the carbon count were 16.
Saturated 18-carbon fatty acid is 18:0; this option would be correct only if the abbreviation were 18:0.

question: Which dietary fatty acid is essential because humans cannot introduce a double bond at the omega-6 position?
cited_learning_objective: Define essential fatty acid and list examples and their food sources

options.rationale: Linoleic acid is an essential ω-6 fatty acid and must be obtained from plant-based foods as stated.
Oleic acid is a monounsaturated ω-9 fatty acid that is not essential; it would be correct only if humans lacked the ability to synthesize ω-9 bonds.
Arachidonic acid is derived from linoleic acid and is not classified as an essential dietary fatty acid in the lecture; it would be correct only if dietary arachidonate were required.
Palmitic acid is a saturated fatty acid commonly synthesized by the body; it would be correct only if the stem asked about saturated fats.
α-Linolenic acid is an essential ω-3 fatty acid, not an ω-6; it would be correct only if the question asked about omega-3 essentiality.

question: How does increasing the number of cis double bonds in a fatty acid affect its melting temperature?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how melting temperature changes based on chain length and saturation

options.rationale: The lecture states that melting temperature decreases with increasing number of double bonds, as seen with oleic and linolenic acids.
Melting temperature increases with chain length, not with more double bonds; this option would be correct only if chain length increased instead.
Double bonds alter packing and lower melting point; this would be correct only if the double bonds were trans and compensated by other factors.
The lecture gives predictable trends; unpredictability would be correct only if structural data were missing.
No biphasic trend is described; this would be correct only with additional context about chain length changes.

question: Identify the configuration and typical dietary origin of most naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids.
cited_learning_objective: Identify trans and cis unsaturated fatty acids and understand health impacts of trans fatty acids

options.text: Cis configuration, plant and fish oils
options.rationale: Most natural unsaturated fatty acids are cis; ω-3s are found in fish and plant oils as noted in the lecture.
Trans fats are usually produced by chemical hydrogenation, not naturally abundant in cold-water fish; this would be correct only if the stem specified industrial processing.
Hydrogenation produces trans fats; cis configuration predominates in unprocessed plant oils, so this is incorrect unless hydrogenation preserved cis bonds.

While some trans isomers can occur in ruminant fats, the lecture emphasizes industrial hydrogenation as the main source of trans fats; this would be correct only if ruminant-derived trans fats were the focus.
Red meat contains more saturated fats; cis unsaturated fats are more characteristic of plant and fish oils and this option would be correct only if specifying monounsaturated content.

question: Which molecule is phosphatidic acid missing compared with other common phospholipids?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and functions of phospholipids and what separates phosphatidic acid from other phospholipids

options.rationale: Phosphatidic acid lacks an additional organic molecule attached to the phosphate; other phospholipids have head groups like choline or serine.
Phosphatidic acid is built on a glycerol backbone; this would be correct only if the molecule were a sphingolipid.
Phosphatidic acid contains fatty acids at carbons 1 and 2; this would be correct only if the molecule were a lysophospholipid missing one tail.
Phosphatidic acid includes a phosphate at carbon 3; this would be correct only if the stem described diacylglycerol.
Ester bonds link fatty acids to glycerol in phosphatidic acid; this would be correct only if the molecule were a sphingosine-based lipid.

question: A patient has progressive neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, and a macular cherry-red spot. Which enzyme deficiency best explains accumulation of sphingomyelin in lysosomes?
cited_learning_objective: List the enzyme deficiency and its usual products for Niemann-Pick Disease

options.rationale: Niemann-Pick disease results from sphingomyelinase deficiency, causing sphingomyelin buildup and the described clinical features.
Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease with glucocerebroside accumulation; it would be correct only if Gaucher clinical signs were present.
Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs with GM2 ganglioside accumulation; it would be correct only if the stem lacked hepatosplenomegaly.
Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy with sulfatide accumulation; it would be correct only if demyelination without hepatosplenomegaly were emphasized.
α-Galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease with ceramide trihexoside accumulation; it would be correct only if angiokeratomas and neuropathic pain were described.

question: Which structural component differentiates a ceramide from sphingosine?
cited_learning_objective: List the components of a sphingolipid, including the differentiation of ceramide and sphingosine

options.text: An amide-linked fatty acid on the amino group
options.rationale: Ceramide is sphingosine with an attached fatty acid at the NH2 (amide linkage), distinguishing it from free sphingosine.

options.text: A phosphate group on the terminal hydroxyl
options.rationale: A phosphate on the terminal hydroxyl yields sphingomyelin when combined with choline; this would be correct only for sphingomyelin, not ceramide.

options.text: A sugar head group attached to the amino
options.rationale: Glycosphingolipids have sugar head groups attached to ceramide's terminal hydroxyl, not to the amino; this would be correct only for cerebrosides or gangliosides.
Glycerol backbone characterizes glycerophospholipids, not sphingolipids; this would be correct only if the lipid were a phosphatidylglycerol.

options.text: An esterified fatty acid at carbon 1
options.rationale: Esterified fatty acids at glycerol carbons define phosphoacylglycerols; this would be correct only for glycerol-based phospholipids.

question: Which phospholipid is especially important in mitochondrial membranes and energy conversion?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and functions of phospholipids and what separates phosphatidic acid from other phospholipids

options.rationale: Cardiolipin (diphosphatidylglycerol) is noted as essential in mitochondrial membranes and plays a role in respiration and energy conversion.

Phosphatidylcholine is a common membrane phospholipid but the lecture specifically highlights cardiolipin for mitochondrial function; this would be correct only if general membrane structure were asked.
Phosphatidylserine is important for membrane signaling and apoptosis, not specifically mitochondrial energy conversion; it would be correct only if the stem targeted signaling roles.
Phosphatidylethanolamine is a major membrane lipid but not singled out for mitochondrial respiration in the lecture; it would be correct only with different emphasis.
Phosphatidylglycerol is a precursor to cardiolipin but cardiolipin is the mitochondrial-specific lipid; this would be correct only if precursor roles were asked.

question: Which pathway converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins and thromboxanes?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: The cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway produces prostaglandins and thromboxanes from arachidonic acid as described.
The lipoxygenase pathway yields leukotrienes, not prostaglandins or thromboxanes; it would be correct only if leukotriene synthesis were asked.
The cytochrome P450 pathway forms epoxides from arachidonic acid; it would be correct only if epoxide synthesis were the target.
Phospholipase C generates diacylglycerol and IP3, not eicosanoids; it would be correct only if signaling lipid cleavage were asked.
Sphingomyelinase degrades sphingomyelin to ceramide; it would be correct only in a sphingolipid catabolism context.

question: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits which enzyme to reduce thromboxane and prostaglandin synthesis?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how aspirin inhibits eicosanoid synthesis

options.rationale: Aspirin acetylates and irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase, blocking prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis.
Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membranes; aspirin acts downstream on COX, so this would be correct only if PLA2 were the target.
5-Lipoxygenase produces leukotrienes; aspirin inhibits COX, not 5-LOX, so this would be correct only if leukotriene synthesis were inhibited.
Cytochrome P450 forms epoxides from arachidonic acid; aspirin does not inhibit this enzyme and this would be correct only with different drug action.
Thromboxane synthase converts prostaglandin endoperoxides to TXA2; aspirin blocks upstream COX, so this would be correct only if the drug targeted that enzyme directly.

question: Which fatty acid listed is a precursor for prostaglandin synthesis and is 20 carbons long with four double bonds?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: Arachidonic acid is 20:4(5,8,11,14) and is the precursor for prostaglandins and other eicosanoids.
Linoleic acid is 18:2 and a precursor to arachidonic acid but is not itself the 20:4 precursor; it would be correct only if conversion steps were emphasized.
α-Linolenic acid is 18:3 (ω-3) and not the 20:4 arachidonate; it would be correct only if ω-3 pathways were the focus.
Oleic acid is 18:1 and not a 20-carbon tetraene; it would be correct only if monounsaturated fatty acids were asked.
Stearic acid is 18:0 saturated and not a precursor for prostaglandins; it would be correct only if saturated fatty acids were the topic.

question: Which lipid class contains a glycerol backbone, two fatty acid tails, and a phosphate-linked head group?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and functions of phospholipids and what separates phosphatidic acid from other phospholipids

options.rationale: Phosphoacylglycerols (glycerophospholipids) have glycerol, two fatty acids at carbons 1 and 2, and a phosphate-linked head group at carbon 3.
Triacylglycerols have three fatty acids esterified to glycerol and lack a phosphate head group; this would be correct only if the stem omitted phosphate.
Sphingomyelins are sphingolipids with phosphocholine on ceramide, not glycerol-based; this would be correct only if sphingosine backbone were specified.
Glycosphingolipids have sugar head groups on ceramide and lack glycerol backbones; this would be correct only if sugars were the focus.
Isoprenoids/steroids are built from isoprenyl units and lack glycerol and fatty acid tails; this would be correct only in a steroid context.

question: A lipid with a sphingosine backbone plus a phosphocholine head group is best classified as which molecule?
cited_learning_objective: List the components of a sphingolipid, including the differentiation of ceramide and sphingosine

options.rationale: Sphingomyelin is ceramide with a phosphocholine head group and is a key component of myelin as described.
Ceramide is sphingosine plus a fatty acid but lacks the phosphocholine head group; this would be correct only if no head group were attached.
Glucocerebroside is a glycosphingolipid with a glucose head group, not phosphocholine; it would be correct only if a sugar head group were present.
Phosphatidylcholine is glycerol-based with choline on phosphate, not sphingosine-based; it would be correct only if glycerol backbone were present.
Gangliosides are complex glycosphingolipids containing sialic acid, not phosphocholine; this would be correct only if sialic acid were specified.

question: Which statement best describes the dietary and health associations of saturated fatty acids per the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the basic structure of fatty acids and be able to give the abbreviation of fatty acids based on chain length and saturation

options.text: Found in animal fats and linked to increased LDL
options.rationale: The lecture notes saturated fatty acids are often found in animal fats and diets high in them are associated with increased LDL and cardiovascular disease.

options.text: Found mainly in fish and reduce LDL
options.rationale: Fish are richer in ω-3 unsaturated fats; this would be correct only if referring to ω-3 fatty acids rather than saturated fats.

options.text: Produced only by plants and increase HDL
options.rationale: Saturated fats are common in animal products; plant-derived unsaturated fats are associated with HDL increases, so this is incorrect unless the stem targeted plant oils.
Saturated fats are typically solid at room temperature due to higher melting points; this would be correct only for short-chain saturated fats.

options.text: Contain cis double bonds in natural form
options.rationale: Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds; this would be correct only for unsaturated fatty acids.

question: Which enzyme releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids to initiate eicosanoid synthesis?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, providing substrate for eicosanoid synthesis.
Cyclooxygenase converts free arachidonic acid into prostaglandin endoperoxides but does not release arachidonate from membranes; it would be correct only for downstream conversion.
Lipoxygenase acts on free arachidonic acid to form leukotrienes; it does not liberate arachidonate from phospholipids and would be correct only downstream.
Phospholipase C cleaves phosphatidylinositol to DAG and IP3, not releasing arachidonic acid; it would be correct only in a different signaling context.
Sphingomyelinase degrades sphingomyelin to ceramide; it does not release arachidonic acid and would be correct only for sphingolipid catabolism.

question: Which eicosanoid promotes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: PGI2 (prostacyclin) is noted to inhibit platelet aggregation and promote vasodilation in the lecture.
TXA2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction; it would be correct only if the stem asked about pro-aggregatory eicosanoids.
LTB4 is a neutrophil chemotactic agent, not primarily a vasodilator or anti-aggregant; it would be correct only if chemotaxis were asked.
PGF2α increases uterine tone and vascular effects but is not the primary inhibitor of platelet aggregation; it would be correct only with different functions.
Epoprostenol is a synthetic prostacyclin analog with similar effects, but the lecture specifically names PGI2; this would be correct only if synthetic analogs were acceptable.

question: Which lipid modification increases cholesterol solubility for storage and transport?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and function of cholesterol

options.rationale: Cholesterol can be esterified at the hydroxyl of carbon 3 with a fatty acid, which is important for cholesterol storage and transport.
Phosphorylation is not the described modification for cholesterol storage; this would be correct only if discussing phospholipids.
Cholesterol is not converted into sphingolipids; this would be correct only in a hypothetical pathway not covered in the lecture.
Hydrogenation of rings is not the storage modification described; esterification is the correct storage form.

options.text: Attachment of a sugar head group
options.rationale: Glycosylation is not the standard cholesterol storage modification; this would be correct only for glycosphingolipids.

question: Which fatty acid abbreviation corresponds to linoleic acid?
cited_learning_objective: Define essential fatty acid and list examples and their food sources

options.rationale: Linoleic acid is abbreviated 18:2(9,12) as listed in the lecture table.
18:3(9,12,15) corresponds to α-linolenic acid (ω-3), not linoleic acid; it would be correct only if the stem asked for α-linolenate.
20:4(5,8,11,14) is arachidonic acid; it would be correct only if the stem targeted arachidonate.
18:1(9) is oleic acid, a monounsaturated fatty acid; it would be correct only if oleate were asked.
16:0 is palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid; it would be correct only if palmitate were the target.

question: A patient consumes a diet high in industrially hydrogenated vegetable oil. Which lipid change is most likely to increase in their serum and is linked to cardiovascular risk?
cited_learning_objective: Identify trans and cis unsaturated fatty acids and understand health impacts of trans fatty acids

options.rationale: Industrial hydrogenation produces trans fatty acids, and diets high in trans fats are linked to elevated cholesterol and cardiovascular disease.
Cis polyunsaturated fats are decreased by hydrogenation; this option would be correct only if the diet favored unprocessed plant oils.
Hydrogenation primarily converts unsaturated to trans or saturated long-chain fats; short-chain saturated fats would increase only with specific dairy intake.
ω-3s are typically found in fish and are not increased by hydrogenation; this would be correct only if the diet included more fish.
Monounsaturated cis fats are not the primary product of industrial hydrogenation; this would be correct only if partial hydrogenation preserved cis monounsaturates.

question: A researcher measures melting points of three fatty acids: 10:0 at 31.6°C, 18:0 at 69.6°C, and 18:1(9) at 16°C. Which structural factor explains the lowest melting point of 18:1(9)?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how melting temperature changes based on chain length and saturation

options.text: Presence of a cis double bond disrupting packing
options.rationale: Cis double bonds introduce kinks that reduce tight packing and lower melting temperature, explaining why 18:1(9) melts at 16°C.
18:1 has the same chain length as 18:0; a shorter chain would lower melting point but is not the case here.
Trans bonds allow tighter packing and higher melting points; this would be correct only if the double bond were trans.
A polar head group pertains to phospholipids, not free fatty acids; this would be correct only if the molecule were a phospholipid.
Esterification forms acylglycerols and alters physical properties, but the melting point comparison here is among free fatty acids; this would be correct only if comparing triacylglycerols.

question: A newborn screening suggests a lysosomal storage disorder with macrophages showing 'crumpled tissue paper' cytoplasm. Which accumulated lipid and enzyme pair fits this finding?
cited_learning_objective: List the enzyme deficiency and its usual products for Niemann-Pick Disease

options.rationale: Niemann-Pick disease involves sphingomyelinase deficiency leading to sphingomyelin buildup and characteristic macrophage appearance.
Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease with Gaucher cells, not the crumpled tissue paper of Niemann-Pick; it would be correct only with Gaucher-specific findings.

options.text: GM2 ganglioside accumulation from hexosaminidase A deficiency
options.rationale: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs with neuronal storage and cherry-red spot but not macrophage sphingomyelin accumulation; it would be correct only if hepatosplenomegaly were absent.

options.text: Sulfatide accumulation from arylsulfatase A deficiency
options.rationale: Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy with demyelination, not the described macrophage morphology; it would be correct only with leukodystrophy signs.

options.text: Ceramide trihexoside accumulation from α-galactosidase A deficiency
options.rationale: α-Galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease with angiokeratomas and neuropathic pain, not crumpled tissue paper macrophages; it would be correct only with Fabry features.

question: Which lipid class is amphipathic and forms bilayers due to hydrophilic head groups and hydrophobic tails?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and functions of phospholipids and what separates phosphatidic acid from other phospholipids

options.rationale: Phospholipids have hydrophilic phosphate-containing head groups and hydrophobic fatty acid tails, enabling bilayer formation.
Triacylglycerols are nonpolar storage lipids lacking hydrophilic head groups and do not form bilayers; this would be correct only if asking about energy storage.
Sphingolipids can be amphipathic and are membrane components, but the canonical bilayer-forming class described is phospholipids; this would be correct only with sphingolipid-specific context.
Isoprenoids/steroids are largely hydrophobic and do not form bilayers; this would be correct only if discussing membrane fluidity modifiers.
Eicosanoids are signaling lipids derived from arachidonate and are not structural bilayer components; this would be correct only if signaling roles were asked.

question: Which dietary source is specifically noted as rich in α-linolenic acid (an essential ω-3 fatty acid)?
cited_learning_objective: Define essential fatty acid and list examples and their food sources

options.rationale: The lecture lists plant oils such as flax seed as sources of α-linolenic acid (ω-3).
Red meat is richer in saturated fats like palmitic acid; it would be correct only if the stem asked about saturated fat sources.
Butter contains saturated fats and is not a primary source of α-linolenic acid; it would be correct only if dairy-derived short-chain fats were targeted.
Cold-water fish provide other ω-3s (e.g., EPA/DHA), but α-linolenic acid is emphasized in plant oils like flax; this would be correct only if the question asked about long-chain ω-3s.
Hydrogenated oils produce trans fats and are not sources of α-linolenic acid; this would be correct only in a different dietary context.

question: Which lipid-derived mediator is primarily responsible for neutrophil chemotaxis?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: LTB4 is identified as a neutrophil chemotactic agent in the lecture diagram and notes.
PGI2 inhibits platelet aggregation and causes vasodilation, not neutrophil chemotaxis; it would be correct only if anti-aggregatory effects were asked.
TXA2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, not neutrophil chemotaxis; it would be correct only with a different function focus.
PGE2 has roles in inflammation and vasodilation but is not the primary neutrophil chemoattractant listed; it would be correct only with broader inflammatory context.
Epoprostenol is a prostacyclin analog with vasodilatory and anti-aggregatory effects, not neutrophil chemotaxis; it would be correct only if synthetic analogs were acceptable.

question: A patient with low-dose aspirin therapy benefits from reduced risk of recurrent myocardial infarction primarily because aspirin irreversibly inhibits which platelet-related process?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how aspirin inhibits eicosanoid synthesis

options.rationale: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase, reducing thromboxane A2 synthesis in platelets and thereby decreasing platelet aggregation.

Prostacyclin is produced mainly by endothelial cells and inhibits aggregation; aspirin affects COX in both cell types but antiplatelet benefit is due to reduced TXA2, so this would be correct only if endothelial PGI2 were the dominant effect.
Leukotriene synthesis is via lipoxygenase and not the primary target of aspirin; this would be correct only with a drug inhibiting 5-LOX.
Aspirin does not inhibit PLA2; it acts on COX downstream, so this would be correct only with corticosteroid therapy.
Phosphatidylcholine synthesis is unrelated to aspirin's antiplatelet effect; this would be correct only in a different metabolic context.

question: Which lipid class is synthesized from isoprenyl units and forms steroid hormones and bile acids?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and function of cholesterol

options.rationale: Isoprenoids/steroids are built from isoprenyl units and include cholesterol, steroid hormones, and bile acids as described.
Triacylglycerols are glycerol esters of fatty acids and do not form steroid hormones; this would be correct only if storage lipids were asked.
Phospholipids form membranes and signaling molecules, not steroid hormones; this would be correct only in membrane context.
Sphingolipids are sphingosine-based membrane lipids, not isoprenoid-derived steroids; this would be correct only if neural membrane components were the focus.
Eicosanoids are derived from arachidonic acid and act as signaling molecules, not steroid hormones; this would be correct only if signaling lipids were targeted.

question: Which glycosphingolipid contains at least one sialic acid residue and has a complex oligosaccharide head group?
cited_learning_objective: List the components of a sphingolipid, including the differentiation of ceramide and sphingosine

options.rationale: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids with complex oligosaccharide head groups that include sialic acid (NANA).
Cerebrosides are simpler glycosphingolipids with a single sugar head group; this would be correct only if a single-sugar glycosphingolipid were asked.
Sphingomyelin has a phosphocholine head group, not sialic acid-containing oligosaccharides; it would be correct only if phosphocholine were specified.
Phosphatidylinositol is a glycerophospholipid with inositol head group, not a glycosphingolipid; this would be correct only in glycerol-based lipid context.
Glucocerebroside is a cerebroside with a glucose head group and lacks sialic acid; it would be correct only if a single glucose head group were the focus.

question: Which fatty acid from the lecture is most likely to be liquid at room temperature due to multiple cis double bonds?
cited_learning_objective: Describe how melting temperature changes based on chain length and saturation

options.rationale: Linolenic acid (18:3) has multiple cis double bonds and a low melting point (−11°C), making it liquid at room temperature.
Stearic acid is saturated with a high melting point (69.6°C) and is solid at room temperature; it would be correct only if saturation were asked.

Oleic acid is monounsaturated with a higher melting point (16°C) than linolenate and may be liquid at room temperature but is not the most unsaturated example; it would be correct only if single unsaturation were emphasized.
Palmitic acid is saturated and typically solid at room temperature; it would be correct only if short saturated chains were considered.
Lignoceric acid is a very long saturated fatty acid and would be solid at room temperature; it would be correct only if chain length effects were the focus.

question: A patient with a mutation causing absent sphingomyelinase activity would most likely show which inheritance pattern?
cited_learning_objective: List the enzyme deficiency and its usual products for Niemann-Pick Disease

options.rationale: Niemann-Pick disease is described as having an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern in the lecture.
Autosomal dominant inheritance is not described for Niemann-Pick; this would be correct only if a dominant sphingolipidosis were specified.
X-linked recessive inheritance applies to some lysosomal disorders like Fabry disease, not Niemann-Pick; it would be correct only with different enzyme deficiency.
Mitochondrial inheritance is unrelated to lysosomal enzyme deficiencies; this would be correct only if a mitochondrial disorder were described.
Multifactorial inheritance involves multiple genes and environment and is not the pattern for Niemann-Pick; it would be correct only with complex trait evidence.

question: Which lipid class includes molecules that act as local regulators derived from arachidonic acid?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: Eicosanoids are lipid-based compounds derived from arachidonic acid that function as local regulators and signaling molecules.
Triacylglycerols are storage lipids and not local signaling regulators; this would be correct only if energy storage were the focus.
Phosphoacylglycerols are membrane lipids and not the primary arachidonate-derived signaling mediators; this would be correct only if membrane structure were asked.
Isoprenoids/steroids are hormone precursors and membrane components, not arachidonate-derived local regulators; this would be correct only in steroidogenesis context.
Glycosphingolipids are membrane components with sugar head groups, not eicosanoid signaling molecules; this would be correct only if glycan-mediated recognition were asked.

question: Which structural feature is common to all fatty acids described in the lecture and gives them acidic properties?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the basic structure of fatty acids and be able to give the abbreviation of fatty acids based on chain length and saturation

options.rationale: Fatty acids are carboxylic acids with a carboxyl group that imparts acidic properties (pKa ~4.8) as noted.
Phosphate groups are features of phospholipids, not free fatty acids; this would be correct only for phospholipid head groups.
Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids, not a universal fatty acid feature; it would be correct only in sphingolipid context.
The steroid nucleus is characteristic of cholesterol and steroids, not fatty acids; this would be correct only for isoprenoids.
Glycerol backbones are present in acylglycerols and phospholipids, not in free fatty acids; this would be correct only for glycerol-based lipids.

question: A patient with decreased mitochondrial cardiolipin content would most likely have impaired which cellular process?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and functions of phospholipids and what separates phosphatidic acid from other phospholipids

options.rationale: Cardiolipin is essential in mitochondrial membranes and plays a role in mitochondrial function including respiration and energy conversion.
Extracellular lipid transport involves lipoproteins and cholesterol esterification, not cardiolipin; this would be correct only if lipoprotein pathways were disrupted.
Membrane asymmetry involves phosphatidylserine and other phospholipids, not specifically cardiolipin; it would be correct only with different phospholipid defects.
Sphingomyelin synthesis pertains to sphingolipids and myelin, not cardiolipin; this would be correct only if sphingolipid enzymes were defective.
Bile acid formation involves cholesterol modification, not cardiolipin; this would be correct only if cholesterol metabolism were impaired.

question: Which lipid is formed when a fatty acid is esterified to the hydroxyl group at carbon 3 of cholesterol?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and function of cholesterol

options.rationale: Cholesterol esterified at the hydroxyl of carbon 3 with a fatty acid forms a cholesteryl ester, important for storage and transport.
Phosphatidylcholine is a glycerophospholipid with choline head group, not an esterified cholesterol; it would be correct only in phospholipid context.
Sphingomyelin is a sphingolipid with phosphocholine on ceramide, not a cholesterol ester; it would be correct only if sphingosine backbone were present.
Triacylglycerol is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids, not cholesterol ester; it would be correct only if glycerol backbone were involved.
Cardiolipin is a diphosphatidylglycerol in mitochondria, not a cholesterol ester; it would be correct only in mitochondrial membrane context.

question: Which enzyme pathway is selectively targeted by celecoxib according to the lecture diagram?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: Celecoxib is indicated in the lecture diagram as a COX-2 selective inhibitor, distinguishing it from nonselective NSAIDs.
Nonselective NSAIDs inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2; celecoxib is COX-2 selective, so this would be correct only for drugs like ibuprofen.
5-LOX inhibitors (e.g., zileuton) block leukotriene synthesis; celecoxib targets COX-2, not 5-LOX, so this would be correct only with a different drug.
Glucocorticoids inhibit PLA2 indirectly; celecoxib inhibits COX-2 downstream, so this would be correct only for corticosteroids.
Leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast) block leukotriene receptors, not COX-2; this would be correct only for those agents.

question: Which fatty acid listed in the lecture table is a 24-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid with a double bond at carbon 15?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the basic structure of fatty acids and be able to give the abbreviation of fatty acids based on chain length and saturation

options.rationale: Nervonic acid is listed as 24:1(15), a 24-carbon monounsaturated fatty acid with a double bond at carbon 15.
Lignoceric acid is 24:0 (saturated) and lacks a double bond; it would be correct only if saturation were specified.
Arachidonic acid is 20:4 and not 24:1(15); it would be correct only if a 20-carbon tetraene were asked.
Oleic acid is 18:1(9) and not a 24-carbon fatty acid; it would be correct only if an 18-carbon monounsaturate were targeted.
Palmitoleic acid is 16:1(9) and not 24:1(15); it would be correct only if a 16-carbon monounsaturate were asked.

question: A patient with inflammatory asthma is prescribed montelukast. Which pathway or target does this drug antagonize according to the lecture diagram?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: Montelukast is listed as a leukotriene receptor antagonist, blocking leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction.
5-LOX inhibitors like zileuton block leukotriene synthesis; montelukast blocks receptors, so this would be correct only with zileuton.
COX inhibitors (aspirin, NSAIDs) affect prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis, not leukotriene receptors; this would be correct only with NSAID therapy.
PLA2 inhibition reduces arachidonate release and is achieved by corticosteroids, not montelukast; this would be correct only with steroid therapy.
Thromboxane receptor antagonists target platelet aggregation pathways, not leukotriene-mediated bronchospasm; this would be correct only in antiplatelet contexts.

question: Which statement best contrasts phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylserine head groups?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the structure and functions of phospholipids and what separates phosphatidic acid from other phospholipids

options.text: Choline head group versus serine head group
options.rationale: Phosphatidylcholine has a choline head group while phosphatidylserine has a serine head group, distinguishing their head-group chemistry.
Both phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylserine are glycerophospholipids with glycerol backbones; this would be correct only if comparing glycerol to sphingosine lipids.

options.text: No phosphate group versus phosphate present
options.rationale: Both contain phosphate groups; this would be correct only if contrasting neutral lipids like triacylglycerols.

options.text: Single fatty acid tail versus two fatty acid tails
options.rationale: Both have two fatty acid tails esterified at carbons 1 and 2; this would be correct only for lysophospholipids.

options.text: Sialic acid-containing head versus choline head
options.rationale: Sialic acid-containing heads characterize gangliosides, not phosphatidylserine; this would be correct only when comparing glycosphingolipids.

question: Which lipid-derived mediator increases uterine tone and is listed among prostaglandins in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Describe briefly the synthesis of eicosanoids from arachidonic acid and list their functions

options.rationale: PGF2α is listed as increasing uterine tone among prostaglandins in the lecture diagram.
PGI2 promotes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation, not uterine tone; it would be correct only if vasodilation were asked.
TXA2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, not primarily uterine tone; it would be correct only with platelet-focused stems.
LTC4 affects bronchial tone and vascular permeability, not uterine tone; it would be correct only in bronchospasm contexts.

PGE1 has vasodilatory and other effects but PGF2α is the prostaglandin specifically noted for uterine tone in the lecture; this would be correct only with different prostaglandin functions emphasized.

question: Which lipid class is described as amphipathic with both polar and nonpolar components and serves as a major fuel source in the body?
cited_learning_objective: List the major classes of lipids, and their basic function

options.rationale: Fatty acids are amphipathic molecules with a hydrophilic carboxyl head and hydrophobic tail and are used as fuel in the body.
Cholesteryl esters are storage/transport forms of cholesterol and are not the primary fuel source; this would be correct only in lipid transport contexts.
Cardiolipin is a mitochondrial membrane phospholipid important for respiration, not a primary fuel; it would be correct only if mitochondrial function were asked.
Gangliosides are complex glycosphingolipids involved in cell recognition, not major fuels; this would be correct only in neural membrane contexts.
Triacylglycerols are major energy stores but are nonpolar and not amphipathic; this would be correct only if the stem emphasized storage rather than amphipathicity.

question: Which clinical feature is specifically associated with Niemann-Pick disease in the lecture and helps distinguish it from Tay-Sachs?
cited_learning_objective: List the enzyme deficiency and its usual products for Niemann-Pick Disease

options.rationale: Niemann-Pick disease features sphingomyelin accumulation in lysosomes with hepatosplenomegaly, distinguishing it from Tay-Sachs which lacks organomegaly.
Isolated neurodegeneration without hepatosplenomegaly is more characteristic of Tay-Sachs; this would be correct only if organomegaly were absent.
Angiokeratomas and neuropathic pain are features of Fabry disease, not Niemann-Pick; this would be correct only with Fabry-specific findings.
Gaucher disease presents with glucocerebroside-laden macrophages and bone involvement, not the sphingomyelin accumulation of Niemann-Pick; this would be correct only with Gaucher features.
Metachromatic leukodystrophy involves sulfatide accumulation and demyelination, not sphingomyelin-laden macrophages and organomegaly; it would be correct only with leukodystrophy signs.
